_meta.notes: Comprehensive index for Bolivia covering Tiwanaku civilization, Aymara kingdoms, Inca Kollasuyu, Potosí silver mountain (richest city in the world, mita forced labor, ~8 million dead), Túpac Katari rebellion, independence 1825 (named for Bolívar), War of the Pacific 1879-84 (lost coast), Chaco War 1932-35, 1952 National Revolution, Che Guevara killed 1967, Evo Morales (first indigenous president), coca/cocaine politics, and lithium reserves.

religion.note: Strongly syncretic Catholicism blended with Andean beliefs (Pachamama, Inti); Virgen de Copacabana; Urkupiña festival; evangelical growth; Aymara yatiri (traditional healers); coca leaf central to spiritual practice

ethnic_groups.notes: Mixed Indigenous-European; culturally dominant middle class; identity fluid (some identify as indigenous in census, mestizo socially)

ethnic_groups.name: Quechua

ethnic_groups.name: Aymara
ethnic_groups.notes: Indigenous; highlands/altiplano; La Paz, Oruro; Túpac Katari (hero, quartered 1781); El Alto (largest indigenous city in Americas); cholita culture; powerful unions

ethnic_groups.name: White (European descent)
ethnic_groups.notes: Spanish descent; historically ruling elite; Santa Cruz elite ('Camba' identity); mining/landowning oligarchy

ethnic_groups.name: Guaraní
ethnic_groups.notes: Lowland indigenous; Chaco region; distinct from highland peoples; Ava Guaraní

ethnic_groups.name: Chiquitano

ethnic_groups.notes: 36 recognized indigenous nations including Moxeño, Guarayo, Tacana, Uru-Chipaya (oldest ethnic group, Lake Poopo); TIPNIS protests

ethnic_groups.name: Afro-Bolivian
ethnic_groups.notes: Yungas region (tropical valleys); descendants of enslaved Africans brought to Potosí mines; ~25,000; Saya music/dance; recognized 2009 constitution

country_profile.notes_unique: Landlocked (lost coast to Chile in War of Pacific 1879-84, still demands sea access); Potosí (Cerro Rico, 'Rich Mountain', richest silver deposit in history, ~8M died in colonial mines); La Paz highest capital (~3,640m); Salar de Uyuni (world's largest salt flat, lithium reserves); Tiwanaku (pre-Inca civilization); Che Guevara killed in Bolivia 1967; Evo Morales (first indigenous president 2006-19); coca leaf ('sacred leaf', not cocaine); world's largest lithium reserves; 2019 political crisis; El Alto (satellite city, 4,150m); ch'alla rituals

910.name: Tiwanaku and Pre-Columbian Highland Civilizations
910.description: The great pre-Columbian civilizations of the Bolivian altiplano — from early settlement around Lake Titicaca through the monumental Tiwanaku state that dominated the central Andes for centuries, its mysterious collapse, and the Aymara kingdoms (señoríos) that followed.

sub_clusters.name: Early Titicaca Basin Cultures: Chiripa and Wankarani
sub_clusters.description: The earliest complex societies around Lake Titicaca, including Chiripa (c. 1500 BCE) and Wankarani on the altiplano. These cultures developed raised-field (suka kollus) agriculture, camelid herding, and ceramic traditions that laid the foundation for the later Tiwanaku state.

sub_clusters.name: The Tiwanaku Civilization
sub_clusters.description: Tiwanaku (Tiahuanaco) became the dominant polity of the south-central Andes, centered on its monumental capital near Lake Titicaca at 3,850 meters elevation. The city featured the Akapana pyramid, Kalasasaya temple, and the iconic Gateway of the Sun. At its height (c. 600–1000 CE), Tiwanaku controlled territories from southern Peru to northern Chile and influenced distant regions through trade and colonization. Its collapse c. 1100 CE remains debated — likely linked to prolonged drought.
key_events: Tiwanaku monumental center flourishes c. 500–1000 CE
Gateway of the Sun carved — iconic Andean monument
Tiwanaku state collapses c. 1100 CE — possibly due to prolonged drought

sub_clusters.name: Aymara Kingdoms (Señoríos) After Tiwanaku
sub_clusters.description: After Tiwanaku's collapse, multiple Aymara-speaking kingdoms (señoríos) — including the Colla, Lupaca, Pacajes, and Charca — emerged across the altiplano. These warring polities built hilltop fortifications (pukaras), maintained extensive camelid herds, and controlled vertical archipelago exchange networks spanning coast to jungle.

920.name: Inca Conquest and Spanish Arrival
920.description: The Inca Empire's conquest of the Aymara kingdoms, incorporating the Bolivian altiplano into Kollasuyu, followed by the Spanish conquest and the discovery of Potosí — the silver mountain that would reshape the global economy.

sub_clusters.name: Inca Conquest of Kollasuyu
sub_clusters.description: The Inca rulers Pachacuti and Topa Inca Yupanqui conquered the Aymara kingdoms after fierce resistance, particularly from the Colla and Lupaca. The altiplano was incorporated into Kollasuyu (the southern quarter of Tawantinsuyu). The Incas imposed mita labor obligations, established tambos, and relocated populations (mitmaqkuna), but Aymara language and identity persisted.
key_events: Pachacuti defeats the Colla kingdom c. 1450
Kollasuyu integrated into Inca Empire — southernmost quarter of Tawantinsuyu

sub_clusters.name: Spanish Conquest and the Discovery of Potosí
sub_clusters.description: Spanish conquistadors reached Upper Peru (Alto Perú) following the fall of the Inca Empire. In 1545, indigenous herders discovered the Cerro Rico (Rich Mountain) of Potosí — the largest silver deposit in the world. The city of Potosí was founded and within decades became one of the largest and wealthiest cities on earth, with a population rivaling London and Paris.
key_events: Discovery of Cerro Rico silver deposits at Potosí — 1545
Potosí founded — grows to become one of the world's largest cities

930.name: Colonial Upper Peru: The Silver Colony
930.description: Upper Peru as the economic engine of the Spanish Empire — the Potosí silver mines powered by mita forced labor, the Audiencia de Charcas, indigenous resistance including the great 18th-century rebellions, and the first cries for independence in the Americas.

sub_clusters.name: Potosí, the Mita, and the Silver Economy
sub_clusters.description: Viceroy Francisco de Toledo institutionalized the mita system (1573), forcing indigenous communities to provide rotational labor in Potosí's mines. Millions of indigenous and African enslaved workers died in the brutal mining operations. Potosí's silver financed Spanish imperial wars and flooded global markets — the phrase 'vale un Potosí' (worth a Potosí) entered the Spanish language. Mercury amalgamation increased yields but devastated workers' health.
key_events: Viceroy Toledo institutes the mita forced labor system — 1573
Potosí produces over half the world's silver supply in the 17th century

sub_clusters.name: Indigenous Rebellions and Túpac Katari
sub_clusters.description: Bourbon tax increases and continued exploitation sparked massive indigenous revolts. Túpac Katari (Julián Apaza) led an Aymara siege of La Paz for 184 days in 1781, nearly capturing the city before his capture and execution by quartering. Tomás Katari led simultaneous revolts in Chayanta. These uprisings, coordinated with Túpac Amaru II's revolt in Peru, represented the most serious challenge to Spanish rule.
key_events: Túpac Katari besieges La Paz for 184 days — 1781
Execution of Túpac Katari — 'I will return as millions' — November 15, 1781

sub_clusters.name: First Cries of Independence: Chuquisaca and La Paz
sub_clusters.description: The uprisings of Chuquisaca (May 25, 1809) and La Paz (July 16, 1809) were among the earliest independence movements in Spanish America. Pedro Domingo Murillo led the La Paz junta before being captured and executed. These revolts predated most other independence movements on the continent.
key_events: Chuquisaca uprising — May 25, 1809 (first in South America)
La Paz uprising under Murillo — July 16, 1809

940.name: Independence, Caudillos, and the War of the Pacific
940.description: The prolonged independence war in Upper Peru, the creation of Bolivia named for Simón Bolívar, the turbulent caudillo era, the catastrophic War of the Pacific that cost Bolivia its Pacific coast, and the silver-tin mining oligarchy.

sub_clusters.name: The Independence War and the Republic of Bolívar
sub_clusters.description: Upper Peru was the last region of South America to be liberated, after 16 years of guerrilla warfare (the republiquetas). Antonio José de Sucre won the decisive Battle of Ayacucho (1824) and the Battle of Tumusla. Bolivia was declared independent on August 6, 1825, named after Simón Bolívar who drafted its first constitution. Sucre served as the first constitutional president.
key_events: Bolivia declares independence — August 6, 1825
Named after Simón Bolívar; Sucre becomes first president

sub_clusters.name: Caudillo Era and the Peru-Bolivia Confederation
sub_clusters.description: Andrés de Santa Cruz formed the Peru-Bolivia Confederation (1836–1839), which was destroyed by Chilean military intervention. Bolivia experienced chronic political instability with over 40 coups in its first century. The caudillo Mariano Melgarejo (1864–1871) epitomized the era's authoritarian misrule.

sub_clusters.name: The War of the Pacific: Bolivia Loses Its Coast
sub_clusters.description: Bolivia allied with Peru against Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879–1884), fought over nitrate-rich Atacama Desert territories. Chile's decisive victory cost Bolivia its entire coastal department of Litoral, rendering it a landlocked nation — a loss that remains a defining national grievance. Bolivia has sought a sovereign access to the sea ever since.
key_events: War of the Pacific begins — February 1879
Bolivia permanently loses Pacific coast access — Treaty of Valparaíso 1884

950.name: Tin Barons, Chaco War, and the 1952 Revolution
950.description: The tin oligarchy's dominance, the disastrous Chaco War with Paraguay, the revolutionary MNR government of 1952 that nationalized mines and enacted agrarian reform, and Bolivia's early Cold War politics.

sub_clusters.name: The Tin Oligarchy and the Rosca
sub_clusters.description: Bolivia's economy became dependent on tin exports controlled by three 'tin barons' — Simón Patiño, Carlos Víctor Aramayo, and Mauricio Hochschild — who formed the Rosca (oligarchic ring). Patiño became one of the world's wealthiest men. Indigenous laborers worked in horrific mining conditions, and political power remained concentrated in the hands of the mining-export elite.

sub_clusters.name: The Chaco War with Paraguay
sub_clusters.description: Bolivia and Paraguay fought the Chaco War (1932–1935) over the Gran Chaco region, suspected to hold oil reserves. Despite larger forces, Bolivia suffered a humiliating defeat — over 65,000 Bolivians died, and Paraguay gained most of the disputed territory. The war radicalized a generation of soldiers and intellectuals, directly leading to the 1952 revolution.
key_events: Chaco War begins — June 1932
Bolivia's defeat — over 65,000 Bolivians killed; Paraguay gains Chaco territory

sub_clusters.name: The National Revolution of 1952
sub_clusters.description: The Movimiento Nacionalista Revolucionario (MNR) under Víctor Paz Estenssoro and Hernán Siles Zuazo seized power in April 1952. The revolution nationalized the tin mines (creating COMIBOL), enacted sweeping agrarian reform redistributing hacienda lands to indigenous peasants, established universal suffrage (enfranchising the indigenous majority for the first time), and expanded education. It was one of Latin America's most transformative social revolutions.
key_events: MNR revolution — April 9, 1952
Tin mines nationalized; universal suffrage established — 1952
Agrarian reform — hacienda lands redistributed to indigenous communities — 1953

950.name: Military Dictatorships, Che Guevara, and Coca Politics
950.description: Bolivia's succession of military dictatorships — including Hugo Banzer's regime, the cocaine-linked 'narco-state' under García Meza, the capture and execution of Che Guevara, and the painful transition to democracy amid hyperinflation and neoliberal shock therapy.

sub_clusters.name: Military Dictatorships and the Death of Che Guevara
sub_clusters.description: General René Barrientos overthrew the MNR in 1964, beginning nearly two decades of military rule. Ernesto 'Che' Guevara attempted to launch a continental guerrilla revolution from Bolivia in 1967 but was captured and executed by the Bolivian army with CIA assistance in La Higuera. Hugo Banzer's dictatorship (1971–1978) was followed by the narco-state of Luis García Meza (1980), whose cocaine-trafficking regime was so corrupt it was repudiated even by other military governments.
key_events: Che Guevara captured and executed in La Higuera — October 9, 1967
García Meza cocaine coup — July 17, 1980

sub_clusters.name: Democratic Transition and Neoliberal Shock Therapy
sub_clusters.description: Democracy returned under Hernán Siles Zuazo (1982), who faced hyperinflation reaching 24,000% annually — one of the highest in world history. Víctor Paz Estenssoro (1985) implemented the New Economic Policy (Decree 21060), a radical neoliberal shock therapy designed by Jeffrey Sachs that crushed inflation but devastated mining communities and provoked the 'Marcha por la Vida' miners' protest.
key_events: Bolivian hyperinflation reaches 24,000% — 1985
Decree 21060 neoliberal shock therapy — August 29, 1985

960.name: Water War, Gas War, and the Rise of Evo Morales
960.description: The social upheavals against neoliberal privatization — the Cochabamba Water War and the Gas War — that propelled Evo Morales and the MAS party to power, making Morales Bolivia's first indigenous president and inaugurating the 'Process of Change.'

sub_clusters.name: The Water War and Gas War
sub_clusters.description: The Cochabamba Water War (2000) erupted when privatization of the city's water system to Bechtel triggered mass protests that reversed the concession. The Gas War (2003) — protests against plans to export natural gas through Chile — forced President Gonzalo Sánchez de Lozada to resign and flee. These upheavals demonstrated the power of Bolivia's social movements and indigenous organizations.
key_events: Cochabamba Water War reverses water privatization — April 2000
Gas War — President Sánchez de Lozada resigns and flees — October 2003

sub_clusters.name: Evo Morales and the Process of Change
sub_clusters.description: Evo Morales, an Aymara coca growers' union leader, won the 2005 election with 54% of the vote — becoming Bolivia's first indigenous president in a country with an indigenous majority. He nationalized hydrocarbons, enacted a new plurinational constitution (2009) recognizing 36 indigenous nations, presided over a commodity-driven economic boom that halved poverty, and championed the Wiphala flag as a national symbol. His insistence on running for a fourth term and disputed 2019 election results precipitated crisis.
key_events: Evo Morales inaugurated as first indigenous president — January 22, 2006
New Plurinational Constitution adopted — 2009
Hydrocarbons nationalized — May 1, 2006

960.name: Contemporary Bolivia: Post-Morales Crisis and Beyond
960.description: The 2019 political crisis surrounding Morales's disputed re-election, his resignation and exile, the interim government of Jeanine Áñez, Luis Arce's election and the return of MAS, and ongoing tensions over democracy, lithium resources, and indigenous rights.

sub_clusters.name: The 2019 Crisis and Áñez Interregnum
sub_clusters.description: After Morales claimed victory in the October 2019 election amid fraud allegations (later debated by international observers), mass protests erupted. The military 'suggested' Morales resign; he fled to Mexico, calling it a coup. Senator Jeanine Áñez assumed the interim presidency in a controversial succession marked by violence, including the Sacaba and Senkata massacres. The events deeply polarized Bolivia and Latin America.
key_events: Morales resigns and flees — November 10, 2019
Jeanine Áñez assumes interim presidency — November 12, 2019

sub_clusters.name: Luis Arce and Bolivia's Lithium Future
sub_clusters.description: MAS candidate Luis Arce won the 2020 election decisively. Áñez was subsequently arrested and convicted. Bolivia's vast lithium deposits in the Salar de Uyuni — among the world's largest reserves — position the country as a potential major player in the green energy transition, though extraction challenges and political divisions persist.
